posts.title: Pick an index for the queries you actually run
posts.body:
Compare a page-based tree with a log-structured design. A tree keeps ordered keys searchable in pages. A log-structured design collects writes in sorted runs and merges them later, shifting some cost to background compaction.

Design check: Compare a point lookup, a time-range scan, and a sustained write burst. Measure p99 latency while compaction is running.

posts.title: Give analytical scans a different layout
posts.body:
A query that aggregates three fields across millions of rows can read less data when values for each field are stored together. Row-oriented storage fits queries that usually load or update most fields of a single record.

Design check: Compare fetching one invoice with calculating monthly revenue across every invoice. List the bytes each query actually needs.

posts.title: Decide what a write acknowledgment promises
posts.body:
With asynchronous replication, a leader can acknowledge a write before followers receive it. A promoted follower can lack that write. Waiting for a replica strengthens the acknowledgment but adds latency and can block writes when the required replica is unavailable.

Design check: Take the leader offline immediately after it acknowledges a write. State which copies must contain the write after failover.

posts.title: Let users read their own writes
posts.body:
A follower can serve an older version immediately after the leader accepts an update. Where users expect to see their own changes, route those reads to the leader or require a follower to catch up to the recorded write position.

Design check: Save a profile change and immediately reload from a lagging replica. Specify which guarantee the user should see.

posts.source: DDIA (1st ed.) · 8 · The Trouble with Distributed Systems
posts.title: Treat a timeout as an unknown outcome
posts.body:
When a service times out, the request might never have arrived, or the operation might have finished before the reply was lost. For operations that must happen once, use a stable request ID and record it alongside the effect so a retry can return the recorded result.

Design check: Drop the response after a payment is recorded. Verify that resending the request returns the original result without creating a second charge.

posts.source: DDIA (1st ed.) · 8 · The Trouble with Distributed Systems
posts.title: Use fencing tokens to reject stale workers
posts.body:
A worker can pause long enough for its lease to expire, then resume after a replacement has acquired the lease. A monotonically increasing fencing token lets the resource reject an older worker after it has seen a newer token.

Design check: Pause worker A, promote worker B, then let A resume. Verify that the storage layer rejects A's write after accepting B's.
